Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed with Sayyed Shahid Hossain, Advocates—For the Appellant. 
MI Faruqui with M Saleemullah, Advocates—For the Respondents.
parties:
Kazi Musharraf Hossain ------ Plaintiff-Appellant
vs
Al-haj Aziz Ahmed and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Abdul Karim J: This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff is directed against the Judgment and decree dated 19-8-1992 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 502 of 1985 dismissing the suit for specific performance of contract. 

 6. Before the trial Court evidence, both oral and documentary, was adduced on behalf of both sides. The trial Court was of the opinion that the plaintiff could not prove that the defendant No. 1 had any authority to enter into any agreement for sale of the suit property on behalf of the other defendants, and defendant No. 1 was not sole owner of the property as described in schedule ''A'' and schedule ''B'' to the plaint. The plaintiff defendant No.1 not being the sole owner of the property of schedule ''A'' and schedule ''B'' the parties were under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement. The Court also observed that the plaintiff having failed to pray for recession of the contract in his suit for specific performance of contract under section 37 of the Specific Relief Act is not entitled to any compensation under section 38 of the said Act or return of the earnest money. With this finding the learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit. Aggrieved by this Judgment and decree the plaintiff has preferred this appeal. 

 7. Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, learned Counsel appearing for the plaintiff-appellant, has submitted that the trial Court ought to have decreed the suit in view of the admitted fact that the defendant-respondent No. 1 S. Aziz Ahmed entered into the agreement for sale of suit properties. He submits that the trial Court ought to have decreed the suit particularly with regard to schedule ''A'' to the plaint inasmuch as the contract, so far as it relates to this schedule, stands on a separate and independent footing from the other part of the contract relating to the property of schedule ''B'' and, as such, the trial Court has committed an error of law in not directing specific performance of the property of schedule ''A''. He has further submitted that the trial Court misconceived the provisions of sections 13, 14 and 20 of the Contract Act with regard to a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement. 

 8. Mr MI Farooqui, learned Advocate for the defendant-respondents, in upholding the impugned Judgment and decree has submitted that the trial Court was absolutely right in refusing specific performance in view of the failure of the plaintiff to prove that defendant No. 1 entered into an agreement to sell the properties on behalf of other defendant and this is clear from the position taken by the defendants in their written statement that they never empowered defendant No. 1 to enter into an agreement on their behalf and that defendant No. 1 is not Managing Director of defendant No. 7 Sambros (Bangladesh) Ltd. The learned Advocate further submits that defendants Nos. 1 to 7 are owners of the property of schedule ''B'' and that defendant No. 1 is not the sole owner of the property of schedule ''A'' and that the contract so far as it relates to schedule ''A'' does not stand on a separate and independent footing from the other part of the contract and, as such, the trial Court rightly dismissed the suit for specific performance of contract. 

 13. Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed has referred to the decision in the case of Archana Prosad Nandi vs Chilia Randolph & others, 1982 BLD (AD) 90. In this reported case for specific performance of contract, the defendants entered into an agreement to sell certain immovable property. The contract was signed by the mother for herself and for her minor daughter and defendant No. 3 step-son of defendant No. 1 signed the contract on his own behalf. Defendant Nos. 1 and 3 signed the contract. The contract is void for defendant No. 2, the minor. It was held by their Lordships that the part of the contract to the extent of two-thirds share of defendant Nos. 1 and 3 stands on a separate and independent footing and taken by itself can and ought to be specifically performed and so the suit was decreed to that extent on payment of the full purchase money and the Judgments of the Court below were set aside. 

 17. Admittedly CS Plot No. 220 as described in schedule ''A'' and schedule ''B'' is a large plot measuring 1.88 acre owned and possessed by six persons and the plot falls in two lots in Schedule ''A'' and four lots in schedule ''B'' and CS Plot No. 219 measures 0.89 acre as described in schedule ''A''. The share of defendant No. 1 is only half (0.44½ acre) in Plot No. 219. Mr MI Farooqui, learned Advocate appearing for the defendants-respondents, submits that section 16 of the Specific Relief Act does not come into play in respect of schedule ''A'' inasmuch as here a part of the contract, taken by itself, does not stand on a separate and independent footing from another part thereof, nor is it such a part of the contract, as can and ought to be specifically performed. In the case of 1982 BLD (AD) 90 (Archana Prosad Nandi vs Chilia Randolph & others), their Lordships laid down two tests to be satisfied before the Court can direct specific performance under section 16 of the Specific Relief Act, Viz, (1) taken by itself a part of the contract can and ought to be specifically performed and (2) its stands on a separate and independent footing from another part of the same contract. It appears from the prayer portion of the plaint as mentioned in paragraph 9(c) that the plaintiff, in addition to a decree for specific performance of contract, also prays for possession of the suit property to be delivered to him through the process of the Court after removing all obstacles and obstructions of the defendants. We already mentioned the plurality of ownership in plot No. 220. There is ownership of two persons who are in ejmali possession in Plot No. 219 also. It is therefore, clear a lot of complications may result from a decree of specific performance with recovery of possession in schedule ''A''. In the instant case, the two tests as laid down in the decision of 1982 BLD (AD) 90 being absent it does not apply to the facts and circumstances of the present case before us. 

 19. In the Judgment the trial Court has mentioned that the plaintiff could have prayed for rescission of the contract in the suit for specific performance of contract under section 37 of the Specific Relief Act to get the relief under section 38 thereof, and that the plaintiff having not done so, the Court was not in a position to pass a decree for return of the money. The simple answer to this is that, it is the contractual obligation of defendant No. 1 as mentioned in clause 9 of the agreement to pay Taka one lac with compensation of Taka 50,000.00 to the purchaser in the event of his failure to induce his brothers and sons to sell the property of schedule ''B'' to him and this obligation cannot be avoided on any plea whatsoever. We, therefore, hold that the plaintiff is entitled to a refund of the earnest money of Taka one lac with compensation of Taka 50,000.00 from defendant No. 1. 

 In the result, the appeal is allowed in part. The Judgment and decree passed by the Court below is set aside. Defendant No. 1 is directed to pay Taka 1,50,000.00 (Taka one lac and fifty thousand) to the plaintiff or deposit the same to the credit of the plaintiff in the Court below within 60 days, in default, the plaintiff will realize the amount through Court with interest @ 12% from the date of institution of the suit till realization.
